title: Hamstring Injury
case: Case: A 23-year-old footballer felt a sudden sharp pain in the back of his right thigh while sprinting and stopped. There is tenderness in the muscle belly, mild bruising, and pain on resisted knee flexion at 15 degrees. No gap is felt. Walking is possible with mild pain. The H-test is limited by pain. No back or nerve symptoms.

Working diagnosis: acute hamstring strain, probably biceps femoris. Plan: early pain-guided loading, bridge and hinge progressions, progressive lengthening exercises, graded running and sprint drills, criteria-based return, and a long-term Nordic and sprint exposure plan.

differentials.name: Hamstring muscle strain
differentials.key: Sudden onset, localised tenderness, pain on resisted flexion

differentials.name: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
differentials.key: Gradual, sit bone pain, worse with sitting

differentials.name: Hamstring avulsion
differentials.key: Sudden severe pain, bruising, gap, unable to walk

differentials.name: Lumbar or sciatic nerve referred pain
differentials.key: Back pain, neurological signs, positive slump

differentials.name: Sacroiliac or deep gluteal pain
differentials.key: Pain near the sacroiliac joint or deep in the buttock

differentials.name: Adductor or other thigh strain
differentials.key: Pain in a different muscle group

differentials.name: Ischiofemoral impingement or deep gluteal syndrome
differentials.key: Pain with hip extension and adduction

qa: Why use criteria instead of weeks? Healing and function differ between people and injuries, so objective criteria are safer than a fixed date.
Why check for a gap and for severe bruising? They can indicate an avulsion that may need early surgical review.
A patient has a stretch-type injury near the sit bone and a long recovery. Why? Stretch-type injuries near the tendon tend to take longer to recover.
Why add lengthening exercises? Hamstrings often fail in a lengthened position at high speed, so training in that position may improve capacity.

How do you tell hamstring pain from lumbar referral? Hamstring pain has local tenderness and pain on resisted flexion, while lumbar referral shows back symptoms and a positive slump with neurological signs.

fields.Position and action: Prone, muscle relaxed, press along the muscle and attachment
fields.Positive: Local tenderness, a gap or a lump; pain that reproduces the familiar pain

fields.Position and action: Prone with the knee bent to 90 degrees; patient pushes the heel toward the buttock against resistance
fields.Positive: Pain or weakness suggests muscle involvement
Pain or weakness; more load on the hamstrings in a lengthened position

fields.Position and action: Prone with the knee straight, lift the leg against resistance
fields.Positive: Pain or weakness near the sit bone suggests a proximal injury

tests.name: Active straight leg raise and passive straight leg raise

fields.Action: The patient lifts the straight leg actively to the pain point, then the therapist raises it passively. Compare with the other side and note where pain begins
fields.Positive: Pain and reduced range compared with the other side; pain at a smaller angle suggests more severe injury
fields.Limits: A reduced range also occurs from nerve irritation; use the slump test to separate

fields.Purpose: Test whether pain or fear of tearing appears in a lengthened position
fields.Position: Supine, the uninjured leg held to the chest
fields.Action: The patient lifts the injured leg quickly toward the ceiling (as if kicking) with the knee straight, to the point of pain or apprehension
fields.Positive: Pain, apprehension or a limited, guarded movement compared with the other side
fields.Supports: Readiness to return to sprinting when a negative test is combined with other criteria

fields.Action: Supine with the hip and knee flexed; slowly straighten the knee while holding the hip bent
Standing, flex the trunk forward with the knee straight and the foot on a support

redFlags.Finding: Sudden severe pain, large bruise, palpable gap, unable to walk, often after a stretch or slide
Severe tense swelling and escalating pain
Numbness, weakness below the knee, foot drop
Back pain with saddle numbness or bladder change
Constant night pain, weight loss, lump

manual.name: Soft-tissue work
manual.application: Gentle after the first days; avoid direct deep pressure on a fresh bruise

manual.name: Neural mobilization
manual.why: May help if nerve irritation contributes

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: early pain-guided loading and criteria-based rehabilitation. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Avoid aggressive stretching of a freshly torn muscle, and avoid deep friction or heavy massage in the first days.

exercise.Exercises: Walking, gentle pain-free isometric knee flexion, bridge (two-leg), heel slides
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 20 to 30 seconds, several times a day
exercise.Progress when: Normal walking pain-free; low pain with isometrics

exercise.Exercises: Bridge progressions (single-leg, feet elevated), hip hinge or Romanian deadlift, slider curl, glute and trunk work
exercise.Progress when: Pain 3 out of 10 or less; no next-day flare

exercise.Exercises: Extender, diver, glider-type exercises (progressive lengthening), Nordic hamstring exercise (when appropriate)

exerciseNotes: Principle: begin loading as soon as pain allows, progress by pain-free criteria rather than by time, and rebuild strength in lengthened positions and running mechanics. Programs that include lengthening exercises have been associated with faster return to sport than conventional programs in some trials.
Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within about 24 hours is generally acceptable. New sharp pain, a new gap or increasing bruising means stop and reassess.

Return to sport criteria (example): full pain-free range of movement, strength of at least about 90 percent of the other leg on testing, a negative H-test or similar test, pain-free sprinting at match speed, and sport drills without apprehension. No fixed time is stated, because severity and site differ.
Prevention: the Nordic hamstring exercise and similar eccentric programs reduce injury rates in team sports, particularly in athletes with prior injury. Add sprint exposure and manage training load.

Proximal hamstring tendinopathy: use progressive loading with isometrics, then bridge and hip hinge progressions, avoiding deep hip flexion stretches and prolonged hard sitting early on. Add running only when sit bone pain settles.
modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): platelet-rich plasma injections have not shown consistent benefit for acute strains. Surgery is considered for complete proximal avulsions or persistent symptoms.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Suspected avulsion or very large tear? Yes: refer for imaging and surgical opinion.
Sudden pain during sprinting or stretching with local tenderness and pain on resisted flexion? Yes: working diagnosis is acute hamstring strain.
Gradual sit bone pain with sitting and loading pain? Yes: working diagnosis is proximal hamstring tendinopathy; use the tendon loading approach.
Start early graded loading and a criteria-based program.
If recovery is slow or atypical, review the diagnosis and consider imaging and specialist opinion.
Visit 1: screen flags and avulsion signs, explain the injury and expected timeline range, start early loading.
Early: pain-guided loading, walking, gentle strength.
